extracted.intended_audience: EPA decisionmakers, rulemaking staff, administrative-law reviewers, and environmental legal advocates
extracted.subtask_description: Notice-and-comment coalition legal comments responding to EPA’s proposed reconsideration/repeal of the 2009 Endangerment Finding and associated vehicle GHG standards, articulating legal, scientific, and procedural standards EPA must satisfy. The document explains statutory interpretation, precedent, administrative-law change rules, scientific evidence standards, and reliance-interest analysis required for a lawful decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Massachusetts v. EPA binding authority / scope of Section 202
rubrics_metrics.description: This issue was decided in Mass v. EPA, which remains binding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Supreme Court held that Section 202 authorizes EPA to regulate greenhouse gases: 'Because greenhouse gases fit well within the Clean Air Act’s capacious definition of “air pollutant,” we hold that EPA has the statutory authority to regulate the emission of such gases from new motor vehicles.' EPA cannot lawfully reinterpret Section 202 to exclude greenhouse gases in the face of that precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: High bar of stare decisis when departing from precedent
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposal fails to acknowledge, let alone clear, the high bar set by principles of statutory stare decisis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an agency proposes a change that departs from settled precedent, it must confront and justify why stare decisis should not control; it cannot simply reinterpret the statute without addressing the binding nature of prior judicial holdings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plain text, context, and practice support Section 202(a) authority over GHGs
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA’s authority under Section 202(a) to regulate 'any' air pollutant, including greenhouse gases, is evident from the plain text and confirmed by context and practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory definitions (e.g., the Act’s definition of 'air pollutant') inform the meaning of Section 202(a). The agency must ground any different reading in text, context, legislative history, or practice—mere policy preference is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cannot narrow Section 202 to 'local or regional' exposure
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA’s effort to narrow Section 202(a) to address only 'local or regional exposure to dangerous air pollution' is baseless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An interpretation that excludes pollutants because they are 'global' rather than 'local or regional' conflicts with the Supreme Court’s reading and the Act’s capacious definition of 'air pollutant' and cannot be adopted without persuasive legal justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Major questions doctrine not a basis for rescinding endangerment finding here
rubrics_metrics.description: The major questions doctrine provides no basis for repealing the endangerment finding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Massachusetts precludes the proposal’s reliance on the major-questions doctrine; the agency must show clear congressional authorization only when the doctrine actually applies. The agency cannot invoke the doctrine to override a Supreme Court holding that the statute is unambiguous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency must not deviate from prior views without adequate explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposal deviates without adequate explanation from EPA’s prior view that regulating greenhouse gas emissions under Section 202(a) does not implicate the major questions doctrine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When changing a long-standing interpretation, the agency must provide a reasoned explanation that acknowledges and responds to its prior rationale and the evidentiary and legal reasons supporting the former position.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulating GHGs under Section 202 does not offend major questions; agency must ask the correct legal question
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulating greenhouse gas emissions under Section 202(a) does not offend the major questions doctrine; 'the proposal asks the wrong question.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proper inquiry is whether the statute, read in context and with applicable precedent, authorizes the regulatory action—not whether the issue is 'major' in policy importance. The agency must demonstrate that the statutory text permits exclusion if it claims the doctrine applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excluding GHGs would undermine AEP precedent
rubrics_metrics.description: Excluding greenhouse gases from Section 202 would undo the basis for the Supreme Court’s conclusion in AEP.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency action must account for related precedent (AEP v. Connecticut) and avoid interpretive changes that would undercut holdings courts have relied on.

rubrics_metrics.name: Endangerment finding can be issued separately from standard-setting
rubrics_metrics.description: The Agency did not err in undertaking the 2009 Finding—which entails a purely scientific inquiry—separately from its development and issuance of vehicle standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 202(a)(1)’s plain language and regulatory history support separating the scientific endangerment inquiry from later regulatory choices; the agency need not conflate fact-finding about endangerment with policy choices about standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cause-or-contribute and endangerment are distinct prongs to be considered separately
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 202(a)(1)’s 'cause or contribute' and 'endangerment' prongs are distinct and merit separate consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The agency must treat the contribution inquiry and the endangerment inquiry as separate scientific/legal questions, and cannot demand concurrent or unitary findings that merge the two without textual support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate definition of the 'air pollutant' includes well-mixed greenhouse gases
rubrics_metrics.description: The 2009 Finding properly considered the relevant 'air pollutant' and 'air pollution' to be the six well-mixed greenhouse gases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA must justify any different identification of the regulated 'air pollutant' with reference to statutory text and scientific evidence; treating GHGs as the regulated pollutant is consistent with statutory definitions and prior practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency must rely on overwhelming, current scientific evidence (NASEM etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Current scientific evidence overwhelmingly supports EPA’s endangerment finding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA must base its factual findings on the best available, peer-reviewed science (e.g., National Academies consensus reports), and cannot substitute cherry-picked or discredited sources to overturn prior findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific claims must be accurate, complete, and not misleading
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposal’s scientific claims are inaccurate, misleading, and incomplete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When asserting scientific conclusions, the agency must accurately represent the state of the literature, explain contrary evidence, and avoid reliance on selective, non-peer-reviewed, or methodologically flawed analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency must reconcile or explain divergence from previous EPA findings
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposal’s scientific claims conflict with previous EPA findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An agency changing course must meaningfully engage with the earlier record, explain why prior conclusions are no longer tenable, and show how new evidence supports the change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Even under alternative statutory interpretations, conclusions must be rationally supported
rubrics_metrics.description: Even considered within EPA’s flawed interpretation of Section 202(a), EPA cannot rationally conclude that the scientific evidence does not support finding endangerment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regardless of interpretive framing, the agency must articulate a rational connection between the facts found and the choice made; mere assertion that evidence is insufficient is inadequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency information quality and peer review standards must be met
rubrics_metrics.description: The Draft CWG Report fails to meet federal standards for data quality and scientific integrity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA must follow federal information quality guidelines and peer review requirements when relying on scientific reports; failure to meet those standards undercuts any claim to deference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance with FACA for advisory committees
rubrics_metrics.description: DOE and EPA’s secretive establishment and use of the CWG violates FACA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies must comply with the Federal Advisory Committee Act’s transparency, fair-balance, public meeting, and records disclosure requirements when creating or using advisory groups whose outputs inform rulemaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courts will not defer to agency reliance on flawed/secret reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts will not defer to EPA’s reliance on the Draft CWG Report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the agency’s underlying process or sources violate statutory or procedural requirements (e.g., FACA, information-quality rules), courts should not grant Chevron or other deference to conclusions based on those sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency must meet the standard for policy change (arbitrary and capricious review / State Farm)
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed reconsideration of the Endangerment Finding violates fundamental principles of administrative law and is therefore arbitrary and capricious and must be rescinded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under State Farm and related precedent, an agency changing policy must (1) provide a reasoned explanation for the change, (2) consider reliance interests, (3) consider the relevant evidence, and (4) not be internally inconsistent or ignore contrary findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency must not unlawfully disregard evidence before it
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA unlawfully disregards evidence before the Agency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The record must be considered: agencies may not ignore or discard significant evidence or expert consensus (e.g., National Academies findings) without reasoned explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency must analyze and weigh reliance interests
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA’s proposal fails to consider the reliance interests associated with the endangerment finding and the vehicles standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The agency must identify affected parties (e.g., automakers, supply chains, consumers), quantify or describe significant reliance interests, and weigh them against policy reasons for change in a reasoned manner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency must consider sector-specific economic impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA must consider impacts on industries such as tourism, real estate, agriculture and fisheries, forests, insurance and reinsurance, and hazardous-chemicals management.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A lawful decision requires sectoral analysis of how rescinding the finding and standards would affect specific economic sectors and related reliance interests, not just generalized claims about compliance costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency must analyze consumer and labor-market impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA neglects consideration of the consumer impacts associated with its proposal and evidence suggests regulations provide labor-market benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consideration must include consumer costs/benefits, preferences for low-emission products, labor-market effects (jobs, worker health), and distributional consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency must consider global political impacts & technology diffusion
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA must adequately assess global political consequences and the U.S. role in technology diffusion and signaling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The agency should analyze how domestic regulatory reversal affects international climate policy, technology adoption abroad, diplomatic relations, and U.S. leadership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency must consider national security implications
rubrics_metrics.description: There are numerous national security impacts of greenhouse gas deregulation that warrant meaningful consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessments should include how climate-driven instability, migration, resource competition, and defense costs may be affected by deregulation and should be part of the reliance/impact analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency must consider global trade impacts (CBAM, competitiveness, carbon leakage)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA disregards how reversal of domestic greenhouse gas regulation affects global trade and associated reliance interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysis must include consequences for international competitiveness, exposure to foreign carbon border mechanisms (e.g., CBAM), and risks of carbon leakage and trade retaliation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency must identify and justify any proposed transitional compliance tools
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA notes that 'manufacturers, importers, and sellers have already expended resources complying with GHG emission standards' but claims it has 'adequate regulatory tools to address transitional compliance concerns' without specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If asserting transitional relief or tools to address reliance, the agency must specify the tools, explain how they will operate, and justify why they mitigate reliance interests sufficiently to permit rescission.
